title: Do manufacturing process improvements qualify for R&D credits?
description: Manufacturing process improvements can qualify for the federal R&D credit under IRC § 41 when the project meets every qualified research test.
summary: Manufacturing process improvements can qualify for the federal R&D tax credit under IRC §41, which treats a plant process, machinery or technique for commercial production as a separate business component. U.S. manufacturers qualify only when the project meets every qualified research test, including technological uncertainty and an 80% process of experimentation, and avoids exclusions like routine quality control.

body.text: Manufacturing process improvements can qualify for the federal R&D tax credit under IRC §41, which treats a plant process, machinery or technique for commercial production as a separate business component. U.S. manufacturers qualify only when the project meets every qualified research test, including technological uncertainty and an 80% process of experimentation, and avoids exclusions like routine quality control.
Federal law only (Internal Revenue Code and Treasury Regulations, with IRS administrative guidance). This report is general information, not tax or legal advice.
Summary

Yes. A manufacturing process can be a qualifying "business component" under IRC §41, and the statute treats a plant process, machinery or technique for commercial production as a business component in its own right, separate from the product it makes. A process improvement earns the credit only if the work meets every element of the qualified research definition and is not caught by a statutory exclusion, such as research after commercial production, adaptation, duplication, or routine quality control testing.
The Credit and Its Current Legal Basis
Permanent credit under IRC §41

The credit for increasing research activities is in IRC §41. The Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015 (P.L. 114-113), section 121, permanently extended it. The Senate Finance Committee's section-by-section summary describes section 121 as permanently extending the R&D credit, and the current statute's amendment notes record that P.L. 114-113 removed the former termination provision. Because the credit no longer expires, a manufacturer can plan multi-year process development programs knowing that the credit will be available for each year in which qualified research is performed, subject to the rules discussed below.
How much the credit is worth
The actual benefit depends on the calculation method chosen, the taxpayer's history of research spending, and whether the taxpayer elects the reduced credit under §280C(c). The statutory rates are:

items: Regular credit: 20% of QREs above a base amount (§41(a)(1)), with the base amount computed from a fixed-base percentage and average gross receipts and never less than 50% of current-year QREs (§41(c)).

Alternative simplified credit (ASC): 14% of QREs above 50% of the average QREs for the three preceding taxable years, or 6% of current QREs if the taxpayer had no QREs in any one of those three years (§41(c)(4)).

body.text: Hypothetical example (ASC). A manufacturer has $500,000 of QREs in the current year and an average of $400,000 for the three prior years. Step 1: 50% of $400,000 = $200,000. Step 2: $500,000 − $200,000 = $300,000. Step 3: $300,000 × 14% = $42,000 gross credit, before any other adjustments such as the §280C(c) reduced-credit election. If the same manufacturer had no QREs in any one of the three prior years: $500,000 × 6% = $30,000.
Payroll tax offset for qualified small businesses

Under §41(h), as reflected in the IRS Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025, finalized by the IRS in February 2026), a qualified small business must have gross receipts of less than $5 million for the tax year and no gross receipts for any tax year before the five-tax-year period ending with that year. The elected amount may not exceed $500,000: the original $250,000 cap, which offsets the employer's share of Social Security tax, plus an additional $250,000 for tax years beginning after December 31, 2022, which offsets the employer's share of Medicare tax. The election is made on a timely filed original return (Form 6765), and the credit is then claimed against payroll taxes on Form 8974 attached to the employer's employment tax return.

The statute text, the finalized IRS instructions, and current practitioner guidance published in 2026 all still show "less than $5,000,000," and the statute carries more legal weight than commentary. The $31 million figure belongs to a different rule: the small business gross receipts test for retroactive §174A expensing, discussed below. A manufacturer that relies on the $31 million figure to make a payroll tax election would risk having the election disallowed.
Expensing of 2022–2024 research costs under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act

items: It applies to domestic research or experimental expenditures charged to capital account for tax years beginning after December 31, 2021 and before January 1, 2025. Foreign research expenditures remain subject to 15-year amortization under §174.

The election is available to any taxpayer, not only manufacturers. The remaining unamortized amount may be deducted in full in the first tax year beginning after December 31, 2024, or ratably over the two-tax-year period beginning with that year.

Separately, eligible small business taxpayers (not tax shelters, and meeting the §448(c) gross receipts test, which is $31,000,000 for a tax year beginning in 2025) could elect to apply §174A retroactively to 2022–2024. Rev. Proc. 2025-28 set July 6, 2026 (or the earlier close of the refund statute of limitations) as the deadline to make that election, and related late or revoked §280C(c)(2) elections, on amended returns or administrative adjustment requests. As of this report's date, that deadline has passed, so manufacturers that did not act by then generally cannot use the retroactive path and are left with the all-taxpayer transition election described above.

body.text: For tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, §174A permits domestic research or experimental expenditures, including qualifying manufacturing process development costs, to be deducted currently or, at the taxpayer's election, amortized over not less than 60 months.
Why a Manufacturing Process Can Be a Business Component

Under §41(d)(2)(B), a business component is any product, process, computer software, technique, formula or invention that is held for sale, lease or license, or used in the taxpayer's trade or business. Section 41(d)(2)(C) adds that a plant process, machinery or technique for commercial production of a business component is treated as a separate business component, and not as part of the business component being produced. Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(b)(2) likewise addresses research involving the development of both a product and a manufacturing or other commercial production process. Its practical effect is significant: a manufacturer that makes a mature, unchanged product can still have qualified research if it develops a new or improved way to make that product.

The regulations give manufacturing examples. In Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(c)(10), Example 7, a manufacturer that modifies robotic equipment that is not commercially available for a new valve manufacturing process, using design alternatives, modeling and testing, is not excluded under the adaptation rule, provided the general requirements of §41(d)(1) are met. In Example 1, a tire manufacturer's design work on a new tread-cooling belt for its production equipment may qualify, while the costs of manufacturing, installing and testing the belts after the design met its requirements are excluded. Read together, these examples show where the line falls in a typical process project: the engineering effort to resolve how a new production method or piece of equipment should work can qualify, but routine build-out and installation after the design is settled does not.
The Qualified Research Tests Applied to Process Improvements

Section 41(d)(1) actually states three requirements for each business component, and the permitted purpose rule in §41(d)(3) supplies the fourth element practitioners usually list. In practice, then, a manufacturing process project must satisfy the §174A expenditure test, the technological-in-nature test, the elimination-of-uncertainty requirement, the process-of-experimentation test, and the permitted-purpose rule, and must not fall within any §41(d)(4) exclusion.
Section 174 (now §174A) test

Section 41(d)(1)(A) originally required expenditures that may be treated as specified research or experimental expenditures under §174. P.L. 119-21 amended it to refer to expenditures treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A. Treas. Reg. §1.174-2(a)(1) defines research or experimental expenditures as research and development costs "in the experimental or laboratory sense," meaning activities intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty about developing or improving a product. Under §1.174-2(a)(3), "product" includes a process, technique or pilot model, so process work fits within the definition; nothing in the regulation limits it to basic research. Costs to acquire or improve land or depreciable property are not §174 expenditures (§1.174-2(b)(1)), although depreciation allowances on property used in research can be. For a manufacturer, this means the engineering labor spent designing and testing a new process can qualify, while the purchase price of new production equipment does not.
Technological in nature

The research must seek information that is technological in nature (§41(d)(1)(B)). Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(5)(i) requires the process of experimentation to rely fundamentally on the principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. By contrast, work that relies on business judgment, market research or management science, such as reorganizing shifts or negotiating supplier terms, does not.
Elimination of uncertainty

Under Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(3)(i), uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or its appropriate design. The regulations also make clear that a taxpayer does not need to show that the information it seeks would be new to others in the field (§1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) rejects a "discovery" test).
Process of experimentation

Substantially all of the activities must be elements of a process of experimentation (§41(d)(1)(C)). The regulation describes this as a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result, for example through modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error (§1.41-4(a)(5)(i)). "Substantially all" is met only if 80% or more of the research activities, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, are elements of a process of experimentation (§1.41-4(a)(6)). For a process project, this means the taxpayer should be able to show that it identified the uncertainty, formed hypotheses or design alternatives, tested them, and refined or discarded them based on the results.
Permitted purpose

Research must relate to a new or improved function, performance, reliability or quality (§41(d)(3)(A)). Research relating to style, taste, cosmetic or seasonal design factors does not qualify (§41(d)(3)(B)). Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(8), Example 1, applies this to a color change made for style reasons. For process improvements, functional purposes commonly include higher throughput, tighter tolerances, reduced scrap, improved yield, lower energy use per unit, or greater reliability of production equipment.
Table 1. Qualified research elements applied to manufacturing processes

cells: Engineering costs to resolve uncertainty about a new production process, excluding the cost of depreciable equipment itself
Finite element analysis used to predict failure points in new process tooling
At the outset, available information does not establish whether a new forming process can hold tolerance on a thinner-gauge alloy
Redesigning an assembly flow to improve throughput or reliability, not appearance
Writing and testing alternative CNC programs to find feeds and speeds that hold tolerance on a new part

body.text: Where Qualifying Process Work Occurs in Manufacturing

items: Robotics and automation. Adapting or integrating robotic systems for a new manufacturing application can qualify when it involves uncertainty and experimentation. Regulation Example 7 (modified robotic equipment for a new valve process) supports this. Simply installing a commercially available robot according to the vendor's specifications, without unresolved technical uncertainty, would not.
Control programs. Developing PLC logic or CNC programs where the method to hold part quality is uncertain can qualify, subject to the 80% experimentation threshold.

Tooling and fixtures. Designing and testing custom tooling, molds or fixtures can qualify. Under Example 1, design and testing up to the point the design meets requirements may qualify, but later manufacture and installation do not.
New materials. Determining processing parameters for a new alloy or composite can qualify where the method or design is uncertain at the outset.

Compliance-driven changes. A process change made to meet a regulatory requirement qualifies only on the same terms as any other project: the method must be uncertain and resolved through experimentation. Routine testing performed solely to show that an existing process meets a standard is excluded as quality control.

body.text: When Process Improvements Do Not Qualify
Section 41(d)(4) excludes several activities that are common in manufacturing:

items: Research after commercial production of the business component begins (§41(d)(4)(A); Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(c)(2)). The regulations are narrower: under §1.41-4(c)(10), Example 2, a new project to develop a new or improved business component is not treated as research after commercial production, so a later improvement project can still qualify if it meets the tests. What is excluded is debugging, trouble-shooting and fine-tuning of a component that is already ready for commercial use.

Adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement (§41(d)(4)(B); Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(c)(3)). Example 6 (rail cars built to a customer's seating and materials specification) is not qualified research.
Duplication of an existing business component from a physical examination, plans, blueprints or publicly available information (§41(d)(4)(C); Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(c)(4)).

Surveys, studies and routine testing, including efficiency surveys, management functions, market research, routine data collection, and routine or ordinary testing or inspection for quality control (§41(d)(4)(D); Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(c)(5)–(6)). Regulation §1.41-4(a)(8), Example 2, treats a modified painting process as a separate business component but not qualified research, because the equipment manufacturer resolved the uncertainty and the nozzle testing was routine quality control.
Foreign research conducted outside the United States, Puerto Rico or a U.S. possession is also excluded (§41(d)(4)(F)), which matters for manufacturers that run process trials at overseas plants.

body.text: The shrinking-back rule

The qualified research tests apply first at the level of the discrete business component (Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(b)(2)). If the whole component does not qualify, the tests are applied to the next most significant subset of elements, and so on down to the most basic element of the component. Regulation §1.41-4(b)(3) illustrates the rule with a new carburetor that may qualify on its own when the engine as a whole does not. Applied to manufacturing, an entire new production line may fail the 80% test because most of its elements are standard, while a newly developed sub-process within it, such as a custom curing station, may qualify on its own.
Table 2. Common non-qualifying manufacturing activities

cells: Hourly calibration checks or standard dimensional inspection
Reconfiguring a standard product to a customer's specification using known methods
Reproducing a part from a competitor's sample or published drawings
A non-technical study of shift scheduling to raise output
Manufacturing and installing equipment after its design already met requirements
Process trials run at a plant located outside the United States

body.text: Qualified Research Expenses for Process Projects

In-house research expenses are wages for qualified services, supplies used in qualified research, and amounts paid for the right to use computers in qualified research (§41(b)(2)(A)). Qualified services include engaging in qualified research, directly supervising it, and directly supporting it (§41(b)(2)(B)), so a process engineer, the engineering manager who directly supervises the work, and a machinist who builds test fixtures for the experiment can all generate wage QREs for the time spent on those activities. Supplies exclude land, land improvements and depreciable property (§41(b)(2)(C)); materials consumed in test runs of a new process can qualify, while new production equipment cannot. Contract research expenses generally count at 65% of amounts paid to non-employees for qualified research (§41(b)(3)(A)). For example (hypothetical), $100,000 paid to an outside testing firm for qualified research yields $100,000 × 65% = $65,000 of contract QREs.
Documentation and Form 6765

A taxpayer claiming the credit must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures are eligible (Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(d)). The IRS Audit Techniques Guide on substantiation (published June 2005) says contemporaneous business records should form the basis of an examination, lists project records such as authorizations, budgets, progress reports and test data, and places the burden of proof on the taxpayer.

The credit is claimed on Form 6765, Credit for Increasing Research Activities. The redesigned form asks for business component information in Section G. Current status: the IRS released the final Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025) on February 5–6, 2026, following IR-2025-99 (October 1, 2025). Under those instructions, Section G is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 and required for tax years beginning after 2025, which means calendar-year manufacturers must complete it on 2026 returns filed in 2027. The exceptions are qualified small businesses electing the payroll tax credit, and taxpayers whose total QREs are $1.5 million or less and whose gross receipts are $50 million or less, filing an original return. Where Section G applies, the taxpayer reports business components that together account for at least 80% of total QREs, up to a maximum of 50 business components.

For refund claims (amended returns), the IRS continues to require the information set out in Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F: identification of all business components to which the claim relates, the research activities performed for each, the individuals who performed them, the information each individual sought to discover, and the total qualified wage, supply and contract research expenses. Practitioner reports state that the IRS has extended the 45-day period to perfect a deficient research credit refund claim through January 10, 2027.

Neither the statute nor the regulations require an engineer to prepare a claim; the legal requirement is that the taxpayer substantiate each element. That said, the increased business-component detail now required in Section G, and the technical character of the uncertainty and experimentation tests, mean that engineering input into the preparation of a manufacturing process claim is a practical advantage even though it is not a legal requirement.
Conclusion

Manufacturing process improvements can qualify for the federal research credit. The statute expressly recognizes production processes as separate business components, and the regulations include manufacturing examples that qualify. Qualification turns on the facts of each project: technological uncertainty at the outset, measured by the information available to the taxpayer; a process of experimentation covering at least 80% of the activities; a functional purpose; expenditures that qualify under §174A; and no applicable exclusion such as post-production fine-tuning, customer adaptation, duplication or routine quality control.
